Geography.name: Mount Everest
Geography.definition: Mount Everest is Earth's highest mountain above sea level, located in the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the Himalayas along the border between Nepal and the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. Rising to an officially recognized elevation of 8,848.86 meters (29,031.7 feet), it was formed by the ongoing tectonic collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates.
key_facts: In Nepal, the mountain is known as Sagarmatha ('Forehead of the Sky'), while in Tibet, it is referred to as Chomolungma ('Mother Goddess of the World').
Sir Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and Sherpa mountaineer Tenzing Norgay made the first officially confirmed ascent of Everest on May 29, 1953.
The peak was designated as Mount Everest in 1865 by the Royal Geographical Society upon the recommendation of Andrew Waugh, who named it after his predecessor, Sir George Everest.
The area above 8,000 meters (26,247 feet) on the mountain is known as the 'Death Zone' due to extremely low oxygen levels and high atmospheric pressure risks.

Science.name: Acceleration
Science.definition: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of an object's velocity with respect to time. As a vector quantity, it has both magnitude and direction, occurring whenever an object changes its speed, its direction of motion, or both.
key_facts: In the International System of Units (SI), acceleration is measured in meters per second squared (m/s²).
According to Newton's Second Law of Motion, acceleration is directly proportional to the net force acting on an object and inversely proportional to its mass (F = ma).
Centripetal acceleration directs an object toward the center of a circular path and is calculated using the formula a = v²/r.
The standard acceleration due to gravity near the surface of Earth is approximately 9.81 m/s².

Science.name: Gravitational Force
Science.definition: Gravitational force is a fundamental attractive interaction that acts between any two objects with mass in the universe. Classically described by Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation, it is modernly understood through Einstein's General Theory of Relativity as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy.
key_facts: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation calculates gravitational force using the formula F = G(m1*m2)/r^2, where G is the universal gravitational constant approximately equal to 6.674 × 10^-11 N·m²/kg².
Gravitational force is the weakest of the four fundamental forces of nature, but it dominates at astronomical scales because it operates over infinite distances and is strictly attractive.

Einstein's Equivalence Principle states that the gravitational force experienced locally while standing on a massive body is indistinguishable from the pseudo-force experienced in a uniformly accelerating frame of reference.

On Earth, gravitational force produces a standard surface acceleration (g) of approximately 9.81 m/s², which accelerates all free-falling objects equally regardless of their mass when air resistance is absent.
